utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, all. May have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Tom Hannis and Crispian Smith on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the witness is escorted back to the stand could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trbojevic, you are still on your oath. You may resume your seat. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I would like to resume our discussion of government meetings by showing you Exhibit P239. And with the usher's help, I'll give you a hard copy of this one. And you'll see in a moment, sir, this is from the 39th Session, the meeting held, it appears, on the 14th of July. You were present at this session. And the first item I want to ask you about is on page 5 of your B/C/S, and it's page 6 of the English. Concerns item number 10. It reads: "Decision on establishing a government committee for the investigation of the theft of both public and private property as adopted." You are the president of the commission, it appears, and Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Buha, Mr. Subotic, and Vojin Lale are appointed as members. Did this commission ever manage to function and carry out any of the proposed work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission did not function like that. I don't know exactly why, but Ostojic wasn't a man of that sort of job. Buha was more or less absent all the time, because the foreign minister -- because he was the foreign minister and he was a member of the negotiating commission that negotiated on behalf of Republika Srpska. More or less he was absent all the time. Subotic was the defence minister. Lale was an official in the justice ministry. For the most part that commission didn't really do anything. I remember that Mr. Koljevic, I don't know if we amended or augmented or tried to improve that commission, I know that he tried to do something about it, but in any case nothing was done. There is no material that would indicate that the commission implemented any procedures or any investigation or confirmed any kind of suspicion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I think we'll see reference to that commission again in a couple of future ones. Next could you look at item number 24. This is on page 8 of the English. It's page 7 of your B/C/S, Mr. Trbojevic. And it deals with a letter from the Ministry of Justice and Administration, and there were a couple of conclusions. I'm interested in the second one which was: "That the proposal for postponing of the execution of punishments to thoroughly take in consideration both positive and negative aspects of the proposal and that, based on that, a proposal for the government is prepared." Then it says you and Momcilo Mandic are in charge. Do you recall what that was about, postponing of the execution of punishments?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momcilo Mandic and I did not make any material about that. That's for sure. But it was generally known that people who were sentenced to less severe sentences were not sent to serve the sentence but were released so that they could be mobilised so that they could be in the army or carry out wartime assignments, and that the serving of the sentence was being deferred for later. There was a procedure to defer serving a sentence from the -- in the law before. I don't know if anything was changed and how, but I know that in practice this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next item is on page 8 -- page 9 of the English, I think it's on page 8 under item 26. It's: "The government concluded again that decision on war commissions provokes great doubts and lack in clarity in its application, causing great problems in the field." "It was concluded that it would be proposed to the Presidency to provide its interpretation of the decision or, if necessary, introduce changes and amendments." Are these the war commissions that Dragan Djokanovic was associated with as a war commissioner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this refers to this decision on the forming of the war commissioners offices. I think that this was a sort of controversial decision by its nature, and it involved a group of people that were now supposed to be - I don't know how I can explain that to you - authorised to go to a certain place and to be a representative of the Presidency to help to set up whatever needed to be set up of the local organs of authority. So in a way it would be an inspector in part, an advisory person in part, a kind of authority. They would embody different aspects of authority which actually are inappropriate to put together. And there were some of us who thought that this was an erroneous approach because these commissioners were creating a kind of system of para-state authority that was bypassing the government and the Assembly. This is something that quickly went into effect, but it's not unusual that the government noted that this was creating a bit of indecision and confusing, and I said that I did go to Herzegovina in that situation. So you'll practically find yourself in a situation where you don't even know what you want and you are not able to resolve whatever situation is going on where you happen to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell me if I'm correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 5, 6, said: "... something that quickly went into effect." I think the witness said quite the opposite. If you can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, it's been raised by Mr. Zecevic that perhaps you weren't interpreted correctly. You are recorded as having said: "... creating a kind of system of a para-state authority that was bypassing the government and Assembly. This is something that was -- this was something that quickly went into effect, but it's not unusual ..." Is that what you said, that it quickly went into effect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I said that it was actually taken out of commission very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood from some of the evidence that we've heard and read so far that one of the ideas behind creating the war commissions was because of some dissatisfaction with the Crisis Staffs and how they had been working and relating with the republican level of the government. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that. The contact between the government and the lower levels did not really proceed very much. It wasn't very strong. The government was practically cut off from the lower organs, and there was some attempts go to the municipalities to talk with them, but it was hard to get to that part of the republic so that, more or less, it was hard to get to a certain place. And then the essential information was not available and there was no possibility to influence the course of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It also seemed that the proposed war commissions were objected to by people in the municipality, primarily members of the local Crisis Staffs who wielded some power in those positions and viewed these new war commissions as something that was going to take away that power or reduce that power. Would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably how it was and it must have been seen that way, but these commissions were not formed. There were individuals who were named, so one person with a first and last name would be assigned as the commissioner covering an area of several municipalities. I don't know if there were any commissions formed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We saw evidence that there was an initial proposal for a war commission in Zvornik that did not include Mr. Brano Grujic who had been head of the provisional government or the Crisis Staff in Zvornik up until that time. Were you aware that he was unhappy about that proposed change in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person by the name of Grujic, I never knew him. We probably did meet, but I don't know what he did or what his positions were. Whether he was meant or not meant to enter some organ or body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I just ask for clarification of an aspect relating to this issue. Mr. Trbojevic is testifying that the war commissions were introduced because of dissatisfaction with the Crisis Staffs, but I'm not quite certain about what was exactly the dissatisfaction with the Crisis Staff. Was it either because they were just too independent and too concerned with establishing themselves in powerful positions on a local level, or was it because of the fact that there was insufficient communication and insufficient means of communication between the government and the local authorities. Could you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I hope you followed Judge Harhoff's question and I would just modify it to say, was it either one of those two or something else or some combination of those factors?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a combination of all of these factors. It's for sure that the communication and links were not sufficient and it was essentially a provisional organ and it was supposed to function in a time when regular organs could not function at some republican level, you never know if it's possible to put together a Municipal Assembly or not, so that it could take decisions or it had to be the Crisis Staff that made those decisions. And then you would be in the position of having doubts whether this was necessary at all, if the Municipal Assembly was there in full complement and could work and operate. So there was some disagreement in that aspect. There was information that members of the Municipal Assembly did not agree with decisions of the Crisis Staff. You had party members in the Crisis Staff, to a degree, that was not quite essential in order to step in instead of the Municipal Assembly and do its work. Then you would have the Crisis Staff president who was either the president of the municipality or the president of the party in that area. He carried the seal with him, or the stamp. He was a moveable municipality. And whenever it was necessary, this stamp was used and used, and used endlessly, so you never knew what was happening. The commissioners were supposed to be some sort of link so that you could know who was doing what, that they would try to influence things and introduce some level of order, but the communications were bad, it was not possible for you to come there every day or every week. You would come there once every few months and then you would meet people whom you saw for the first time. You don't know who is who, how they came to that post. Everybody would be telling their own story, that it was terrible, you had nothing to eat. There was no possibility for anything to work, that they needed this and that. And, of course, you couldn't react immediately, you didn't have authority or the possibility to resolve things like that. And thirdly, you had no criteria to be able to tell who is telling the truth, who was a good guy, who was lying. I mean, it was just a system that was untenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, did that clarify it for you or should I make some further inquiry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, no, I'm perfectly satisfied with the answer. But that raises the next question, how on earth was introduction of the war commissions supposed to remedy all those dangers?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was convinced that it could not resolve these things, that you had to insist that the Municipal Assembly works and not these provisional organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The conclusion here was that it be proposed to the Presidency to interpret the decision about war commissions or make some changes and amendments. Did that happen, do you know? Did the Presidency provide an interpretation or make some changes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think things stayed the same for a period of time until the Assembly adopted a decision and then put these things out of commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And last item I want to ask you about in this one, Mr. Trbojevic, is on page 10 of the English, and it's on the last page right above the signatures. It says: "It was concluded that Ministry of Justice and Administration at its first session is to inform the government on the work of the commission for the exchange of prisoners and to propose personnel solutions providing the normal working conditions ..." Do you recall if after this meeting that there was information from the Ministry of Justice about the working of the commission for the exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I ever saw a report like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go next then to the next session. This is Exhibit P240. I'll hand you a hard copy of this one, with the assistance of the usher. And as it's making its way over to you, I will tell you that this appears to be the 40th Session of the government held on, I believe, the 16th of July. You are listed as being present. And the items I want to discuss is the last one, number 8, which is on page 4 of the B/C/S and page 4 of the English. And it's the second or third paragraph. I guess Mico Stanisic is apparently speaking. It says: "Mico Stanisic has made an objection appointing Milan Trbojevic to the post of president of the commission for throwing a light on the plunder of governmental and private property that the government had passed in its last session. As a reason for the objection, he stated that Trbojevic occupied an apartment on Grbavica unjustified and that he did not allow iron from Metalija to be exported to Serbia as compensation for securing foodstuffs for the needs of the MUP." Do you recall that objection made by Mr. Stanisic, and can you give us any further clarification about what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do recall his objection but this related, more or less, to actually questioning my role in the commission because I actually had not ensured that there was this exchange of iron for foodstuffs. Also, it had nothing to do with me appropriating some apartment or anything like that, so that, in fact, no comment was really serious. It really had to do with questioning my place in that commission. But as far as I know, the commission -- as far as I know and as far as I attended the meetings, the commission was really not very successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see two paragraphs down from where I finished reading off that it says: "As for the objection on the reservation on Grbavica, it has been concluded that this matter has to be clarified. It has been stressed that no one can be accused of something until proven guilty." Was there -- did Mico Stanisic ever offer any later government session evidence to back up this claim that you were occupying an apartment in some unjustified fashion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, there was no further discussion relating to that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you -- did you and Mico Stanisic know each other before you started working as the deputy prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We weren't close, in fact, we weren't close associates, but I did meet him a couple of times before the -- on one occasion actually, before the war. So, yes, we did know each other but we weren't -- we didn't work together, we had no ties or no connections of any sort. We weren't on friendly terms, but we were not adversaries either. Simply I knew that he was someone who was an official. He probably knew that I was an attorney but there was no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This -- this allegation against you, though, made in front of the other ministers in a government session, seems to be less than friendly and more adversarial. Do you know any reason why he would have some animosity against you to make that unsupported allegation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my earlier evidence I explained that there was a confrontation and a rift between President Djeric on the one hand and Mico Stanisic on the other hand, and that, as vice-president, I sort of sided with Branko Djeric, as it were, and found myself on the other side vis-a-vis Mico Stanisic. And Momo Mandic, as a former policeman and the man who came from the police circles, he was closer to Mico Stanisic than to us, and he then happened to join, if I may put it that way, that side. So that then we had a situation where it was not possible to communicate well and to co-operate closely, rather there was a rift in our relationship, and perhaps this could have been the reason. Perhaps it was felt that it would be better to remove me and have instead someone who would be less controversial and less opposed to their positions. And of course, after all these years, I can state, although I don't have strong arguments, but that whatever happened was not directed against Mico Stanisic, or rather, if there were instances of misappropriations, of theft, and abuse of power, that it would be a good idea to know who was behind that and to prevent such activities in the future. So that was the extent of my participation in the commission. As I've already said, it wasn't possible to accomplish much. I do know that there were some reports later on regarding some vehicles from TAS at Vogosca. Whether there were any reports on the oil, crude oil from the wartime reserves, I wouldn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the first part of that answer you said that you had previously explained that there was a confrontation and a rift between President Djeric on the one hand and Mico Stanisic on the other hand. Did you ever personally witness a confrontation between Djeric and Stanisic that would reflect that rift?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I came to Pale and when I became a member of that government, I believe that that confrontation, that clash between them had already been evident. I don't know what triggered that. I've already said that I had occasion once to witness a brief -- a brief altercation between the two on a corridor and where at one point he said, You know, if you go on like that I'll arrest you, but then they just parted ways. Of course, I asked Djeric what that was about, but he is a man who doesn't usually finish his conversations. He would just sort of wave his hand and say, Well, never mind, let go. But, you know, I wouldn't want to go into that any further. I didn't want to go into it any further or investigate what that was all about. I didn't see any other such instances, but I did observe that they were -- that their relationship was cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you clarify a couple of things or give me some details about that. In your answer you said: "... at one point he said, You know, if you go on like that I'll arrest you ..." Who said that to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanisic said that to Djeric. I don't know exactly how that went, but that was the general -- he said, you know, something to that effect, I will have you arrested or something like that. I don't know the exact words that he used, but it sounded -- well, the way it sounded, it could be interpreted as a serious matter, but I myself did not think that it was serious really. But then later on, when Djeric tried to reconstruct the government, to reshuffle it, and to have Stanisic removed from the government, there were those efforts and so on and so forth, but that, too, was not brought to fruition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us where this occurred, this confrontation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This confrontation that I just mentioned, this discussion was in Bistrica Hotel. That's where the headquarters, if I may use that term, of the government was at the time. They were on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anyone else present to hear that other than you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were just the two of them, and I just happened to run into them, because I had just left the office where the government was, and the secretary was there and some clerks, or rather, people who were working on the drafting of regulations. On the other side was the lobby of the hotel where somebody must have been. And then by the door, the front door, there was probably a policeman sitting there, but I can't really tell for sure. There would have been some 5 to 6 metres between them and me. And then from the lobby to where they were, there would have also been some 5 to 6 metres, but whether there was somebody sitting there, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which hotel was this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was Hotel Bistrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And their voices? Calm, spoken like you and I talking now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were raised voices and that's what actually drew my attention, and that's why I looked in their direction because I could hear these two voices, high-pitched. They were basically yelling at each other. That's what it looked like. It was very loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what Mr. Stanisic was wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really say with certainty. He frequently wore a uniform, but whether he was in uniform then, I really don't know. I can't say for sure. And Djeric was in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to the last item in this meeting. It's on page 5 of your B/C/S, and it begins at the bottom of page 4 and goes on to 5 in the English. "Mico Stanisic has informed that the making of rules on internal organisation and work of the Ministry of the Interior is in process." He mentioned certain questions that would have to be resolved, in particular that about the authority and co-operation of the organs of the interior and the army. It has been agreed that a meeting between the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Defence, and the Main Staff be held as soon as possible. And going on to page 5 in the English, the last line says: "It has also been agreed that this meeting be organised by the government prime minister." Do you know, sir, if that meeting ever took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know specifically about this meeting, whether it was organised or not, but I can only assume that there were several such meetings because I know that there was talk about establishing joint patrols, joint police and military patrols. And I know that the recurrent problem there was the issue of mobilising police members in the army, or putting them under the command of the army. So these were recurrent problems that were ongoing. And I believe that there were a number of meetings to discuss those issues. Whether this particular meeting was held or not and what the outcome would have been, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go to the next meeting, which is the 41st Session, and I will hand you a hard copy of the minutes for that one. While that's on its way to you, I'll tell you this was a session that occurred on the 22nd of July. It's Exhibit P200. It shows you as being present at this session. And the first point I want to ask you about is found on page 3 of both the English and the B/C/S. And there's some objections that have been raised regarding the minutes of the previous -- or of the 39th Session that had taken place prior to this one. Under number 2, Momcilo Mandic made an objection, and he said that the doubts had been expressed regarding the legitimacy of appointing you to the post of president of the commission for throwing a light on the plunder of social and private property. And he proposed that the president of the commission should be Velibor Ostojic and that Mico Stanisic should be a member of the commission. Do you remember that discussion in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the same discussion that we saw earlier in the minutes, in the other minutes. The objections were the same, that this had do with my being an unsuitable proposal or candidate, that I had prevented this exchange of iron for foodstuffs, and that there should be a commission established to establish whether I had actually appropriated an apartment in Grbavica and so on. So more or less, this is the same story that had been discussed in the earlier meeting. As I've already said, there's nothing I can add to this, to what I said earlier, nor was it me personally, Milan Trbojevic, who actually -- who actually prohibited this exchange of iron for foodstuffs, nor did I move into this apartment. As for the proposal that Mico Stanisic should be the president of this commission, well, that could have been the most reasonable proposal, but because there were some stories going around about some warehouses where stuff was disappeared from them and that this had to do with Stanisic and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure if the witness said Zupljanin as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it would have been logical for him to have been appointed president of that commission and if it was to be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreter noted that they weren't sure what you said at the point where you said there were some stories going around about some warehouses where stuff was disappeared from them and that this had to do with Stanisic, and they didn't catch -- did you mention a second name besides Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did mention Momcilo Mandic also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in light of those rumours or stories going around, it wouldn't be appropriate for Mico Stanisic to be part of the commission investigating, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said it would have been the most logical choice to have the president -- the chief of the police to be at the head of such a commission, but of course, it would have been much better if there was no need for that kind of commission to be set up. But there was gossip that there were some warehouses in Grbavica or around Grbavica. These were police depots, that Mandic and Stanisic were aware of this, and that some goods that were in the warehouses were seized in a manner that would throw some suspicion as to how these goods disappeared. So in the sense that there should be a commission that would investigate that, when I told the two of them about this, they got angry and they said, Well, are you trying to investigate us; whereas my intentions were really to just try and throw some light as to what had happened with those goods because we needed to have strong arguments to show that there was no crime involved there, that perhaps the goods were used for the needs of the army or something. But as I said, it wasn't really my purpose to allege that they were involved in any crime or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 18, 12. I think it says here that there should be a commission and I believe the witness said that it was, in fact, formed something. If you can really see with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, your answer was translated in part as saying: "So in the sense that there should be a commission that would investigate, that's when I told the two of them about this." Did you mean to say that a commission actually was formed or only that it was being discussed that one should be formed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two factors here. I said had it been -- had everything been as it should have been, there would have been no need for such a commission to be established. However, if there was a warehouse that was plundered, that was just -- all the goods were removed from it and so on, then the regular police would have the task. It would be their job to determine -- to establish a commission, and to determine what had happened with the goods. Now, if the commission was to be formed, if we were forming a commission, it would be the most logical thing to have the chief of police at the head of it. But he was not proposed as the head of it probably because of the gossip that had already been circulating around regarding these two depots or warehouses, to the effect that Mandic and Stanisic knew about these depots, that they knew about these goods and perhaps they even knew what had happened with them. So that those --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreters have asked you to repeat the last sentence of your answer, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanisic was probably not proposed as president of that commission, although it would have been the most logical thing for the chief of police or minister of police to be at the head of such a commission. Probably because this commission would have had to establish the actual situation within these two warehouses. I can't recall whose warehouses these were, what companies they belonged to, because there was suspicions that perhaps Mandic and Stanisic knew about what had happened with this -- with these goods and that perhaps they were the ones who were responsible for the goods disappearing from there. So this was the reason why the two of them would not -- or maybe this was the reason why they were not members of this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you've been a judge and a lawyer and a Defence lawyer, would you agree -- I agree with you that, typically, I would expect the chief of police to be involved in investigating this kind of activity. But if there are suspicions that the police may have been involved in the activity, then you wouldn't want to use the police; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One last question about this point. Mr. Ostojic is proposed by Mr. Mandic as a member of the commission, even as president of the commission, and I think you said earlier when we were talking about this commission, you didn't understand what qualifications Mr. Ostojic had for working on such a commission. We know that he was the minister of information, so why did you think he was not an appropriate person for this commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a number of reasons why not. Ostojic was a man, he was a professor, I believe, a professor of liberal arts, someone who had no experience with the police other than on one occasion -- on one occasion his -- they actually smashed -- hurt his head and he ended up in hospital. So for these reasons, he was not the appropriate, the suitable person for this commission, but here he was proposed and then it was like, well, whoever could be a member of the commission. Ostojic was a politician and he was the advocate of the party platform and political -- and he had the political authority as such a person, as a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we have spent enough time on these sort of internal matters at the government level, so unless you are able to convince us that this is relevant, then I think we should move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can understand your bringing that to my attention, Your Honour. I think it's important to see the relationship between particular individuals and particular events that were going on at the time that may support the Prosecution's submissions at the end of the case about what weight to give certain evidence or certain witnesses, motivations of certain persons for doing or not doing certain things at certain times. But if I can ask two more questions on this, then I will move on. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on your working in the government with these other gentlemen, do you have an opinion about the relationship between Velibor Ostojic with Mandic and Stanisic compared to what you've described as the relationship between you and Djeric on the one hand and Stanisic and Mandic on the other?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what their relationship was, their personal relationship. I never witnessed anything, any conversation between them, nor did I ever hear that anything was said in public about their relationship. I can say about Ostojic that vis-a-vis the government, as I've already mentioned earlier, he -- his position, he came from the position of someone who was a member of the party and that all of us who were not members of the party would be replaced soon and so on and so forth, so that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could turn next to page 6 in the B/C/S. It's page 6 of the English. Item number 11. On the occasion of the conclusions by the Presidency, the following had been concluded, I'm interested in the second one, (b): "In connection with a conclusion that the decision to put the police forces reserves under the unitary command of the army be passed, it has been concluded that a state of war has to be announced prior to passing this decision." Can you clarify for us what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see from the text that a decision was requested for the police reserve forces to be placed under the single command of the army, and that the conclusion was that the adoption of such a decision should be proceeded by the declaration of the state of war. So the army was constantly looking for military conscripts and some of them were deployed to the reserve police forces as their wartime assignment, so there was probably a proposal for the reserve police force to be transferred to the military units, and the minister then warned that it is not possible to implement such a decision before a state of war is proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So was it your understanding, then, that in July 1992 in the Republika Srpska, which was then in a state of imminent threat of war, the police reserves could not be put under the unitary command of the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is regulated by the law. I don't know exactly what the law says on that. I'm not going to comment on that. But it is logical what is concluded here, and it seems to be in accordance with the existing provisions of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you to item 14 on page 8 of the English, I'm not sure which page it is for you, but it's the third bullet point. It says: "The government has been appointed on some occurrences of unlawful treatment of war prisoners." Do you recall by whom and how the government was informed about these occurrences of unlawful treatment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I remember specifically this. I see that this was under current affairs and under the group of founding the AAA Automotive Association. I think there was an order here about the treatment of prisoners of war which was probably drafted the way it should have been drafted. I don't know exactly what part of the information this refers to, to which positions. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm somewhat confused by that answer. Do you know how and by whom the government had been informed about the unlawful treatment of war prisoners? Was that in a report, a written report or an oral report, and if so, from which ministry or which individual did that come?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't know. I know that there are several reports in the documents about which I don't know when they were sent. Some don't seem to be authentic by their content, some do indicate that things happened which were not supposed to happen. I don't know what this referred to specifically. I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, was the issue of the conditions for detention of people something that was discussed at the government meetings on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conditions in institutions for detention was not something that was discussed separately. There were existing prisons which were older institutions which functioned in an ordered manner. They functioned the way they functioned, just like they did before the war. They were under the monitoring of the president of the district court, the police and so on. As for these things that were happening about which we were finding out later, that there were some collection centres that existed, that there were camps such as Manjaca, Omarska, this is something that was being learned about later. There were no debates or discussions about that, that they should exist, how they would be provided for and secured, or who would be in charge of that. I know that Kalinic from the Red Cross agreed -- was negotiating how to get into these camps, who was there, what were the conditions there, but the government did not really -- the term of war prisoners is something that would eliminate the government from that entire story. A prisoner of war captured in a military action, in combat, in fighting, by the very nature of the thing would have to be something that had to do with the military units, so some actual information about capturing civilians en masse and bringing them to the collection centres. This is something that we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think this meeting was in late July. Do you recall that it was approximately around the 8th, 9th, 10th of August that the international community became aware of Manjaca camp and some of the other camps and the conditions there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was said that Karadzic had approved visits to Manjaca, and visits to Prijedor, and I remember the television programs after that. I think Mr. Ashdown was in Manjaca, specifically. There was a British TV station that showed pictures from Prijedor and that skinny man in Trnopolje. I heard about this Trnopolje thing in Banja Luka, that this was a place where Muslims were being protected from their own and our extremists, that people would be able to go in and out freely, and that it was a place where they were safe and removed so that other people would not endanger them who were robbing the villages and things like that. I don't know how many people were involved and I don't know that this was something that was discussed at government meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, page 25, 19 to 22. I believe the witness said that the people were put in these in Trnopolje to be protected from the extremist, and that they were allowed to go in and out freely, meaning the people, not the extremists, and now it's totally different in the transcript. I mean, maybe you can clarify that with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the way Mr. Zecevic expressed it was probably what you said. Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, that is so. I saw the footage, I don't know if it was in some case here in The Hague, I don't know, where I could see a woman walking along the road and she was telling the journalists on camera that she was rushing off to Trnopolje to seek refuge there. I don't know if this was edited or who did it, but that was the story that I, as a citizen of Banja Luka, heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd next like to go to P244. I'll hand you a hard copy of this one with the usher's help.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll tell you, Mr. Trbojevic, this is from a government session on the 8th of August. It's noted as the 45th Session. You are present. And two things I want to ask you about in this one. Page 5 of your B/C/S, and it's page 4 of the English, under questions and proposals. I think it's the third paragraph under number 13. Concerning the information that different salaries are being paid to interior ministry organs and in different modes, it was concluded that the Ministry of Interior should issue an order stating that interior ministry organs are to be exclusively funded from the SR BiH budget. And that the salaries of the MUP employees should be adjusted. Can you elaborate on that paragraph any? What kinds of different salaries were being paid and what different modes were they being paid in, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this, believe me. This is something that is totally unknown to me, this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next line said: "It was also concluded that the order should issue a standard MUP uniform while speeding up production of the uniforms." Before this date were there non-standard uniforms being worn by the MUP, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were different uniforms that were ordered through private channels, that were donated by various donors, that there were different insignia on the uniforms, some where there were flags, some were the four Ss, some were the eagles. More or less these -- this insignia was just sewn on to the uniforms. There was no systematic dressing in a particular type of uniform. As far as I know, there was the standard issue blue uniform and the standard issue camouflage uniform in blue camouflage colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have on that meeting. I'd like to go now to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll hand a copy to the usher to trade. This next one is Exhibit 427.13.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's a session held on the 9th of August. It's the 46th Session of government. And it looks like Mr. Djeric was absent and you actually chaired this session. If you could look at page 3 of your B/C/S, and it's in the English page 2. This is the agenda. Item number 12 is agreement to include tour of camps in SR BiH. And I guess for my question I need you to turn to page 5 of the B/C/S. And it's page 4 of the English. You'll see there item 12 states that the government formed two commissions consisting of representatives of the interior judiciary and administration: "The commissions' task is to gain knowledge through responsible state organs about the status of people in concentration centres and other sheltering facilities, to speed up the procedure of categorising these people, establishing responsibility and sanctions." You were the chair of this meeting, can you tell us what these two commissions were and who the members were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why the members of these commissions are not mentioned in the minutes. Usually they would be noted. I don't know who would be in them. I can't remember that now. I can see that the way the task is formulated here to see about the status of people and to speed up the procedure of the categorisation and to gain knowledge about it, this really indicates to what extent the government did not know exactly what this was about. I'm surprised that there are no names of the people who were supposed to be in these commissions. But basically, this talks about facilities to shelter people, the need to categorise the situation and to sanction the people responsible, but what it seems to be is that these were people who had been deprived of liberty for some reason, who had to be processed. But these shelters or collection centres are not actually that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a question about that. My English translation says "to speed up the procedure of categorising these people." Is that a correct translation, categorising these people meaning the people being held in these facilities and centres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably what it says. The procedure of categorising the said people, talking about people who have been placed in collection centres and other sheltering facilities. The term "prison," regular prison is not mentioned here, but this is a formulation of the old government [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I had gathered from our conversations yesterday about --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. I am sorry, 29, 9, I believe it says formulation of the old government. I believe the witness said of the secretary of the government. But maybe you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretary. I did say that this was a matter of the formulation of the secretary of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Meaning Mr. Lakic who wrote the note?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question, though, was: Yesterday, I think we saw some government sessions where there were discussions about the commission for exchange and I think we talked about your impression that you understood that to relate to prisoners of war. I asked you, I think, yesterday, when did you first become aware that in some cases non-Serb civilians were being detained, and I think your answer was sometime in November. My question is about categorising these people in these facilities and centres, and that seems to suggest to me that these are people other than prisoners of war because if somebody is categorised as a prisoner of war, you don't need to do any further categorising because we know what the Geneva Conventions and the international laws require in connection with that. Would you agree with that interpretation, this must mean something other than prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quite right. I thought about what I said yesterday, and thinking about that, I was aware that I had said that I did not hear anything before I came and spent sometime with the citizens. This formulation that a categorisation should be carried out indicates and suggests that there is quite a number of people about whom there is no evidence that they should be deprived of their liberty. It says here that these are organs for placing people into these sheltering and other types of facilities. And it is a fact that they are talking about people that need to be categorised, and logic would seem to indicate that this is not only about categorising criminal acts but whether these are people who participated in combat or in financing or politically supported the enemy side, and so it is closer to the logic that you would have also people here who were there in an attempt to seek shelter or who were deprived of liberty. I don't know how you could describe that generally in some settlement or in some sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know usually break at 10.25, but I wonder if we might break a few minutes early today. This is a convenient point for me. I'm about to go into another one that I need to make some markings on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we rise and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, the next one I want to show you is Exhibit P246. I'll hand you a hard copy. This is from what is described as a closed session of the government held on the 19th of August, immediately following the conclusion of the regular 47th Session. I think I've only seen two occasions where there were closed sessions of the government. Can you tell me, if you recall, why these sessions were closed and was there some provision in the law for having closed government sessions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether there is a provision in the law, probably so, but in this particular case, I don't even know why it was a closed session, who decided upon it. More or less, all these sessions were the same. We were on Mount Jahorina and there was no publicity, as it were, so calling a closed session could only mean that a number of associates who would come with some ministers to these sessions would not attend the sessions. But there was no -- it wasn't closed in the sense that there was any kind of secrecy about it, or anything, so I don't know what the reason could have been for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, on this occasion, the topic appeared to be discussion about the collection centres and the camps. The other one, as I recall, was dealing with discussions about oil, oil reserves. On this one, item number 1 says: "The government will regularly follow the situation in the facilities used for captives, collection centres, investigation centres, and other similar buildings, and through its commissions will assess the state of these buildings and the treatment of the people kept there..." I recall from one of the earlier meetings, weren't you on one of the commissions to do this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I was. I don't know that I was and I know for sure that I did not visit any of these centres, regardless of what type of centre they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the government commissions did do as was concluded here, in terms of follow-up at these camps and centres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you look at page 2 in the B/C/S. We're still on the first page in English at the bottom. Item number 4 says: "The Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior will take measures to ensure that the army ... takes over the task of safeguarding all these facilities." I infer from that that up to this date that someone other than the army, and presumably because this talks about the Ministry of Interior, presumably the police had been involved in guarding some of these facilities. Would that be correct, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty, but whether the police did provide personnel for -- to serve as guards in those facilities, that's very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And still on that page for you and the next page in English at the very top: "The issue of the open collection centre in Trnopolje should also be resolved as soon as possible, and in a way which will enable the quickest possible departure from this area." Do you recall was that so that the people who had been detained there could be removed or taken out of the RS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the purpose for Trnopolje, as far as I can recall, was to provide shelter for people there, and what it says here is that this issue of the open collection centres should be resolved as soon as possible so that they would be able to depart the area as soon as possible. That seems to be consistent with that. But whether these people -- whether what is meant there is that these people would leave Republika Srpska or whether they would return to Prijedor, or to wherever they had come for, I really don't know and cannot conclude from what it says there. Whether there was a general position taken that they should leave the territory of Republika Srpska, there was no such position adopted. But what is meant by this specifically, I really couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like now to show you Exhibit P247. And with the usher's help I'll trade you hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A couple things I would note, Your Honours, in terms of this document is that -- I'm not sure how it is in e-court, but what is page 2 of the document is actually behind page 16 in my hard copy. I think when it was stamped and printed, it was copied in the wrong order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the other thing, Mr. Trbojevic, I know that the date on these minutes on the 48th Session says it was of a meeting held on the 28th of July. However, the date of the minutes appears to be September 9, and I know that the 47th Session that we've just looked at was held on the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says on the 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And the 49th Session apparently was held on the 7th of September, so I am assuming this is a typographical error and the 48th Session was probably on the 28th of August. Would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on this one I just want you to look at page 15. It's the next to the last page before the signature, and it's page 11 in the English. Item number 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess in B/C/S we have to go one page forward. Sorry, page 15 in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 33 says: "The government decided to organise a meeting in Banja Luka on the 29th of August, to include," you, "Dragan Kalinic, Subotic, General Gvero, Avlijas, Stojan Zupljanin, and other Krajina representatives to discuss the situation and agree the disbanding of concentration centres for prisoners. This should be placed in the context of implementing the decision of the London conference, and the Ministry of Information is due to inform the public about this and exploit it for propaganda purposes." Did you take part in such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. It says here Dragan Kalinic, Bogdan Subotic, Avlijas, Gvero. I don't remember attending this meeting so I can't -- I can't claim that I wasn't, with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know, if you weren't there, whether or not the meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say with certainty but I do know that Kalinic went with the Red Cross, that he agreed with the Red Cross, the International Red Cross, on some aspects. I don't know if this was in a meeting with General Gvero -- whether this meeting with General Gvero and Mr. Subotic was just a follow-up on those meetings, but -- and those negotiations with the International Red Cross, but I think there was an agreement on Manjaca, that there would be -- that they would enable the International Red Cross to have access to Manjaca and things like that. So whether it had do with that or not, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall attending any meeting at which Stojan Zupljanin was in attendance, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin and I, well, I've said on a number of occasions that I didn't have any official contacts with him. In one of the meetings where -- when the government was in Banja Luka, he attended one of those meetings, but I don't know that I attended a meeting where -- which he attended also where we discussed some official situation, something that had do with his line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you now another meeting. This is Exhibit P272. All I have are handwritten notes from this meeting. I'll hand you a hard copy. This is described as a government session on the 14th of September in Bijeljina. And it appears that you were in attendance because you are listed as a speaker. When you have that in hand I'll ask you to look at page 5 and -- it's page 6 for you, I guess, and it's page 5 of the English. Do you find where you are at the top as a speaker and the five items under your name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 5 says: "The Law on Internal Affairs in a similar way, minister is tied to the Presidency and the government has no influence." Can you explain what you meant by that? How was the minister tied to the Presidency rather than the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I remember this specific session. I do recall some other sessions held in Bijeljina regarding the London conference. There was an Assembly and government session, and then the Presidency and the government convened a session, and then there was a session where the matter of the government being moved to Banja Luka was discussed. So I remember those, but this particular one I can't really say. But what I've said, what I apparently said here was that there should be more frequent meetings between the government and the Presidency, and that, in my view, there were some very irregular provisions on the Law on the Army and the Law on the Police. I don't know what that referred to. Then I see there's mention made here of the Main Staff and the relationship -- and I see mention of the minister of police who has direct ties with the Presidency and bypasses the government, the government has no influence on him. I think this had to do with the fact that he was more frequently in contact with the president than with the prime minister which, of course, has its history because, of course, he was also in charge of the state security which, by its very nature, is more within the ambit of the Presidency rather than the government. But what the specific trigger for this discussion was on this occasion, I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Farther down on that page, you speak again. You say the government is incomplete. Three ministers are in Belgrade. Can you tell us what you meant by that? Which ministers were in Belgrade and why, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that Vice-President Pejic, who was in charge of finance, had offices in Belgrade. He was in poor health and he did not move easily, so he didn't spend much time in Republika Srpska. I don't know whom else I had in mind, but I do know that everyone tried to spend as much time in Belgrade as possible, because it was preferable being in big city than being on top of a mountain, but I don't know whom I meant here specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Then --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buha was in Belgrade. Stanisic and Mandic, I don't know how much time they spent in Belgrade, but -- so I don't really know which three I was actually referring to here. Antic was in Belgrade, for instance. He spent almost all of his time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me take you next to exhibit -- sorry, I guess it's 65 ter number 1216. I'll give you a hard copy of this one. While that's on its way to you, I will tell you this is a meeting on the 26th of September, 1992. It's the 52nd Session of the government. You are listed as being in attendance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I just wanted to alert you that you have 25 minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I hope to finish by or before then. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about item number 53, which is at page 11 in your hard copy, page 9 of the English. That's a topic entitled "Questions and Proposals." The first one says: "The Ministry of Interior is to prepare a report on security in Republika Srpska for the next government session. The report should focus on theft of socially and privately owned property. After it is verified in a government session, the report shall be discussed in a joint session with the Republika Srpska Presidency. The TAS," T-A-S, the car factory in Sarajevo, "problem shall be discussed at one of the following government sessions." Do you recall, was such a report prepared and presented to the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government that would actually cease to exist in a month or two from that moment on, I think, did not receive that report. There was a report discussed later on, I think, at an Assembly session, but we did not discuss it. And I know that I am deeply convinced that all the facts were not actually cleared up. Those vehicles were stolen. They were gone. The spare parts were stolen, they were gone. Their value was in the millions but we never actually established who was responsible for that and who organised this theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to tender that one, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P428, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And next, Witness, I'd like to show you 65 ter number 1219. I'll also give you a hard copy of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm advised that this one apparently does have an exhibit number, P251. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Trbojevic, I'll tell you these are the minutes of the 55th Session, held on the 12th of October. You are shown as being in attendance. And I want to ask you about item -- an item on page 8 of your B/C/S. It's page 7 of the English. Near the bottom. Says: "The Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Interior Affairs together with the Republika Srpska army's responsible organs are due to criminally prosecute persons who are currently in the Serbian Radical Party's paramilitary formations on charges of draft dodging and other crimes they have committed as a paramilitary formation." What can you tell us about that, do you know what crimes they were alleged to have committed as a paramilitary formation, and whether or not this was carried out and any prosecutions were actually held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this refers to specifically or which paramilitary unit it has in mind, which locations, and what events or incidents. As far as I know, there was no follow-up prosecution or any proceedings where anyone was convicted of any crime. I don't know what this means specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You hadn't heard, either officially or unofficially, about paramilitary formations connected with Seselj or Seselj's radical party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the stories about paramilitary formations and units were plenty. We had problems with them and we received sporadic information regarding incidents involving them, but what this specifically referred to, I really wouldn't know. I know that there was a unit on Grbavica whose leader was, if my memory serves me well, a certain Vojvoda Aljic [phoen]. There was a unit in Vogosca. There was also a unit on Grbavica, I don't know who that belonged to. So there were many paramilitary units, at least there were many stories about various paramilitary units, but I don't know specifically of any particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let me show you next Exhibit P253. And I will tell you, as it's coming around, that this appears to be the minutes of the 57th Session of the government, held on 27 October. Again, as usual, you are shown as being in attendance. And I'd like to have you look at page 6 and that's also page 6 in the English. Item number 22, which reads that: "Momcilo Mandic, Minister of the Judiciary and Administration, has informed the government on the situation in Republika Srpska camps and assembly centres. It is concluded that the existing illegal camps and assembly centres are to be dissolved as soon as possible." I take it from that that as of 27 October, there were still some illegal camps and assembly centres in the RS? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see from here that Mandic is informing about the status or the situation in the camps and the collection centres. This would be my conclusion but I don't know specifically what this refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any information, official or unofficial, at that time about the number or nature of those camps and the persons, the category of persons that were being held there, the conditions, any of that information known to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several reports, and I did say that I didn't know which one arrived when, something of that was known, but I don't know what this report by Mandic specifically referred to. I don't know. This is already late October. The government was already outgoing. Djeric had submitted his resignation. It was known that he was going to submit his resignation. He insisted that this be in the Assembly, that a work -- a report on the work be discussed which would then be followed by his resignation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've been asked if you could repeat the last sentence of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was already actually a phase when the government existed formally. Djeric was known to be about -- to submit his resignation, he was supposed to do it at the Assembly session after his report on work was reviewed, which happened on the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then I want to take you to one final meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 1225. 1225.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll give you a hard copy of that. This one appears to the minutes of the 61st Session of the RS government, held on 21 December. You are present. And the only question I want to ask you about this one is basically this appears to be the session in which the hand-over of the government took place between the outgoing prime minister, Mr. Djeric, and the incoming prime minister, Mr. Vladimir Lukic. Do you recall that session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any specific details. I know that the meeting did take place, and I know that Lukic's government was formally elected, if I'm not mistaken, in January. What we did in December, hand-over of duty, because Lukic's government was elected at the Assembly session, I think, of the 18th of January, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps he handed over the duty to the next prime minister designate who was then about to elect the other members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender 1225.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P429, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And lastly, Mr. Trbojevic, I would like to hand you a hard copy of an excerpt from, this is 65 ter 2653. This is from the minutes or actually, from the transcript of the 20th Session of the RS Assembly, which was held in Bijeljina on the 14th and 15th of September. And if you want to look at the first two or three pages to see that it does appear to be referring to that 20th Session of the Assembly, and I want to direct you to a particular page where you are listed as the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I want to go to page 36 of the English in e-court, and I believe in e-court it's page 40 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For you, Mr. Trbojevic, I think I've put a sticky on the side of the page that I want to direct your attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just to clarify, you said it was 65 ter 2653. In your mail you mention it as 2635.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it 53?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is 53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic kindly pointed out to me that I transposed those numbers and I wrote back, copying everyone I think I'd sent the original, to advise that Mr. Zecevic was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you find that page?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the part I want to read is you talking about -- at the bottom of page 36: "Camps for inmates, prisoners, and civilians and who knows what are opened in republic but no one or most authorities know nothing about them." Yesterday, I think you told me that you thought you only became aware of civilians being detained in November when you started talking to people on the ground and heard about it unofficially. But here we have you in the middle of September speaking in the Assembly making reference to camps for civilians. My question is: Does that refresh your memory about the earliest time you might have learned about civilians being detained in these camps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I'm saying here that camps for prisoners, civilians, detainees, for whoever are being opened across the republic. Nobody from the authorities or the majority of us do not know who is opening these camps. The minister in charge of refugees is stunned when representatives of the Red Cross tell him, Well, there is a camp in such and such a place, is this a state or not? So what I'm saying here is that most of us who were members of the government did not know who was opening camps and I'm wondering how a minister entrusted with the care for refugees does not know if somebody tells him that there is a camp in such and such a place. Of course this is not all right. That was not my point. There were rumours constantly going around, but what a person can know specifically and reliably about specific particulars, this is quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if civilians were being detained in camps run by the army or the police, the minister of refugees wouldn't necessarily be informed about that, would he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who detains someone must take care about that person in any option. Food has to be provided for at least, and then the directorate for commodity reserves would know that food is being required.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would like to tender that Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P430, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, before we pass the word on to the Defence teams, could I just ask you to clarify what these rumours that you heard were about. You said that rumours were circulating around but, of course, you couldn't rely on rumours, but what did the rumours say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult after so many years to say what rumour was heard, in which context, at what place, and there were some suspicious reports which came to the government's attention as well. One of them I looked at and it did not contain any relevant points which would characterise the situation. It spoke about medical and health measures, food and things like that. But then later it would turn out that the situation was quite different. As for what information reached me when, I really couldn't tell you. My first specific information at firsthand was that there was a collection centre in Trnopolje where Muslims were being sheltered. This is the first thing that I heard realistically. Of course it was on television when the international institutions were permitted to enter Manjaca and Omarska. There was footage from Trnopolje, footage from Manjaca, where Mr. Ashdown even commended the way Manjaca was being run. There was a whole bunch of information, but as for the real state of affairs, that was something that a person could hear about only when they became familiar with this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis asked you just a while ago whether you began to be suspicious about what really happened in September or November, I think. But I wasn't sure about your answer. Do you recall when you first had suspicions about what was really going on in the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the fall, September or October, it was clear that the government was falling apart, that it was going to be replaced or disbanded, that our mandate was ending. So the need for a person to officially monitor something or the possibility to have an effect on anything was actually being lost here, and from being in the forefront, it kind of receded towards the back. So I was brought into the situation where, as a regular citizen, I was no longer to say anything to anyone. You cannot really reach and see which military unit was doing something where. It was more important to see if somebody would be mobilised and sent to the front, rather than whether somebody was fulfilling their duties or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just for the record, Your Honours, we are joined, the Stanisic Defence is joined by our legal consultant assistant, Mr. Andreja Zecevic, thank you, who is present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you were a member of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and after the Assembly of Republika Srpska was formed you remained a member of the Assembly of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
