utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, just one request, we need to make a pause. We speak the same language but we need to take into account the interpretation in order to avoid problems with the transcript. Mr. Trbojevic, can you please tell me, you are familiar with the plan of the European Union which was popularly called the Cutileiro plan after the Portuguese foreign minister, Mr. Cutileiro. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't recall the particulars, but I do recall it generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You recall that the plan provided for the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina into three entities with a central government or a federal government headquartered in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember our relief that all three parties to the negotiations reached an agreement, and that this could mean that our expectations would be met and that the war situation would no longer apply. But as for the contents, I do remember that there were three regions at the national level, or according to the ethnic or national level, and they would be united into one state community union.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that this division into three so-called entities, according to the national principle, and that each of those entities, according to the agreement reached on the 18th of March in Lisbon between the representatives of the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, provided for the existence of certain organs of state administration, which would be separate for each entity with one federal ministry in Sarajevo, a headquarters that would cover that particular area. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't confirm and say that I was very familiar with the structure. I know that in the Serbian ranks this was accepted with relief and I know that the public opinion that prevailed was that efforts needed to be made immediately to achieve a real situation in the field that would approach as closely as possible the Cutileiro plan. So this is not an official conclusion by any organ, but this was the prevailing opinion that you could hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the Serbian side was completely in accord what the Cutileiro plan, it accepted it, and tried in the field to adjust the situation in the field in accordance with the solutions from the Cutileiro plan. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course you recall that the plan was signed on the 18th of March, as I just said, actually, it was signed in principle, and then after some time, after a couple of days, Mr. Izetbegovic withdrew his signature to the plan, to these joint principles that were agreed on in Lisbon. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We mentioned the position of the Serbian side. When you said that the Serbian body of the population accepted the Cutileiro plan with relief, is it not true that the position of the Serbian side was primarily guided by the desire to remain in a common federative Republic of Yugoslavia, in a joint Yugoslavia? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The platform that preceded all of this was a firm political position of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina that the final and basic objective was to preserve the unity of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the basic tenet -- that was the basic tenet of the position of the Serbian side, and this Cutileiro plan envisaged -- what it envisaged was a kind of position in reserve that the Serbian side accepted to have Bosnia-Herzegovina leave Yugoslavia but to be divided into three entities according to the national principle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say that it was the forced acceptance of a lesser evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the Dayton Accords from 1995, in essence, accepted with small modifications the basic positions of the Cutileiro plan and this actually came into being and is the reality on the ground today, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Trbojevic, did you know that the SDA, Party of Democratic Action, as early as the 1990s, actually, as early as 1991, called upon members of the Muslim ethnic group not to respond to the call-up to the JNA, not to serve their military term of duty. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that political position. I think that the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina was published on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that along with that position about refusing to respond to the call-up and to serve the military tour of duty, the young men were placed by the SDA into police reserve forces and were sent for training to the Ministry of the Interior in Croatia on the basis of some agreement or under the alleged agreement between the MUP of Croatia and the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually I didn't know that in 1991 and 1992. Today, from these cases that are being tried, I know that there is a lot of evidence in that sense. I mean, this was more or less published, the forming of the Patriotic League and the co-operation and the provisions provided by the Croatian police to the Patriotic League and so on and so forth. There is numerous documentation about this, much more voluminous than what I know. But I did have the opportunity to see these basic things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are aware that other than training they also took part in the combat within the ZNG units; isn't that correct? I mean, you know that now; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some things I did know in 1991 as well. In Kupres, the conflicts in 1991 were between the Croatian units and the Serbian population. And in March 1992, there was an incursion by the Croatian units into Sijekovac, near Brod, and so on and so forth. These were things that were known even then. And after the Storm action and so on, and Flash, they were known.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's make a small digression. You lived in Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the seat of the Party of Democratic Action was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know where that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does Titova Street, Marshall Tito Street mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the main street of Sarajevo. It's the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You don't recall that the seat of the SDA, original seat, was in Marshall Tito Street 7A?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Trbojevic, since you were a member of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were present at the Assembly session on the 15th of October, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, courtroom is too small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Life is dangerous, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is here, 65 ter 1483. You will recall that on this day --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would seek the assistance of the usher to give the witness these minutes from this session. This is document 65 ter 1483.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These are minutes of the 8th joint session of the Chambers of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held over a period of three days, on the 10th, 11th, and 14th October 1991, and which ended in early morning hours on the 15th of October. Do you remember that session, and if I understood you correctly, you actually attended it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did attend it and I'm just trying to get my bearings and see whether the dates as mentioned here are what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, perhaps I can leave the document with you so that you can leaf through it during the break and then I can come back to the question. But tell me now, you surely remember that the declaration on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina was adopted at this session; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was trying to actually find in the minutes. I do remember that I left this -- I walked out of this session together with the Serb deputies because -- and this declaration was adopted in our absence, and we considered that to be at that time, and I still feel the same way, an illegitimate or rather unlawful act.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But as far as I know, the specific aspects of the Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution, because of the fact that there were three constituent ethnic groups there was set up in such a way so that neither one or not one of those ethnic groups would be able to decide on their own, or rather, vote over the decisions that would actually put them at a disadvantage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were actually discussions on amending the constitution to allow for constitutional guarantees which would provide for these vital interests of each of the constituent nations and that they would actually be specified in these constitutional amendments, so that not one of the groups could actually be voted over by the other two. And this was discussed on several occasions before a number of different bodies also in committees, but as far as I know, this job was never actually completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But as you were a member of the Serb caucus in the Assembly, you were on the SDS ballot although you were not a member of the SDS, and you tried through the institutions of the country to block the implementation of this declaration that you considered unconstitutional and unlawful, and you actually sought to accomplish this through legal methods provided for by the constitution, the parliamentary rules, and the rules of parliamentary democracy, all those means that you had at your disposal; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a dead-line given for the submission of a request to have the independence recognised, and I know that within our own Assembly club, the club of the Serb representatives in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we discussed this with a number of experts on constitutional law, how to actually oppose this, and how to fight it, because we were still on the position that we should seek to preserve the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. Although, at the time, the independence, the declared independence by Croatia and Slovenia had already been recognised internationally. So we had these discussions as to how to prevent Bosnia and Herzegovina from officially addressing this matter to the international community, and we concluded that there was no instrument that we could use to efficiently fight this other than a kind of filibuster or obstruction in the Assembly session so that the -- so that we would push the time and have the dead-line expire for this decision. But we realised that, in the final analysis, if our obstruction or filibuster threatened to actually push back the dead-line, that the president of the Assembly would actually just sign this decision and send it to the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Without the approval of the parliament; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and as we saw later on, it was actually adopted in this Rump Assembly, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said during your evidence that sometime in May you left Sarajevo and went to Pale where Mr. Djeric met you and suggested that you become a member of his government, and he said that he would clear this with Krajisnik and Karadzic. And in fact, immediately following this, you accepted that offer and you began your work in the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This government, as we've already seen because you've said this several times, and yesterday you said this on page 4.084 of the transcript, the government fell on the 20th of November and you remained in your post for some one month and a half on doing the technical work until the new government would take over; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We saw today that the new minister designate had already taken his -- taken over on the 21st of December and the new government was proclaimed, or elected I believe you said, at a session on the 18th of January. Yesterday, on page 4.085, Mr. Hannis, my learned friend, asked you something about the war crimes commission, and he read out to you the minutes from a government session of the 3rd of June. This is Exhibit P224. And among other things, it said there that the government concluded that a proceedings should be initiated to investigate the war crimes, and the Ministry of the Interior and the commission for war crimes were actually tasked with this job. Do you recall discussing this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You answered that you could not remember that that commission was established in June 1992, but that the war crimes commission to investigate crimes committed against the Serb population was only established in 1993, and then Mr. Karadzic actually tasked you to be at the head of this commission. But as far as you could recall, it never actually began its work, but rather, it began its work in co-operation with the federal commission for war crimes in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you said at the time that a judge was the -- at the head of this commission and you said that you couldn't recall his name, so I wanted to remind you. Could this be Judge Ilija Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's quite possible. I think he was Ilija, his first name, I know that he was a district court judge. I visited him on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the late Ilija Simic, he was a district court judge in Belgrade. You said here on several occasions, so I wouldn't want to elaborate on that, but you mentioned the government worked under very difficult conditions, that they were on Mount Jahorina. There was no heating, no electric power, that the snow made the things even worse because the roads were not passable, and that you did not have any means of communication. So in effect, the government actually did not have any kind of infrastructure which would enable it to work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We literally did not even have typewriters, no telefaxes, nothing. We would -- if we got hold of one, we would bring it, whatever we could find.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that you mentioned somewhere, but I just want to make sure and verify that with you, were the roads to other parts, to all other parts of Republika Srpska open? Was it possible to communicate via road traffic with other parts of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to go to Banja Luka you had to go travel via Bijeljina, and then along Posavina which is some 500 kilometres. So it was impossible to use the normal road via Travnik, which would be some 200 kilometres, that distance would be some 200 kilometres. And the situation was such up until the end of July, approximately, when the corridor was opened up. The way to Serbia, you had to take the road to Zvornik, then go toward Karakaj. And then at Sekovic that road was cut off because it was within the area of responsibility of some units that were deployed there and that were under fire, so at times this road was passable and at others it wasn't because there was fighting going on. Some villages were burned down there and so on. So as far as I could see, that was the situation. These were the two main roads. As for the others, I don't know exactly how that went. I think the road to Foca was passable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, do you know that the Ministry of the Interior made and invested a lot of effort into ensuring that information was -- flowed in from the field to the centre?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that the ministry, because of the nature of its work, would have had to have connections with their field offices, the police stations and so on. Whether those communications were always possible or not, I don't know, but there must have been some form of communication because the structure of the ministry was such. It was organised in this vertical manner, hierarchical matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to show you now 65 ter 177. This is a communication from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, you didn't tender 65 ter 1483.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours -- no, no, no, I understand. But I suggested to the witness that he reads it through the -- during the break and then I will ask him some more questions, and that is why I didn't want to lose the time. Thank you very much for reminding me. [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness 65 ter 177, please. Could the usher also provide a hard copy to Mr. Trbojevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, this is a document from the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo. The date is 18th of July, 1992, and this information was forwarded to all security centres. And it was to the chief, personally, and it was signed by the minister, Mr. Stanisic, and he is requesting information regarding all significant information of security interest, the situation, the security status on robberies, profiteering, and other serious criminal offences. And he also instructs, in the second paragraph, that such information should be sent every day by 1900 hours, and then at the end he adds in hand: "Non-compliance with the order shall constitute a serious breach of the work obligation in time of war," and so forth, "and I will immediately and energetically take all measures necessary in order to establish who is responsible." From this it arises, no doubt, that there were many difficulties in this flow of information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct, because otherwise it wouldn't be necessary to actually provide specific instructions, and it was specifically mentioned there that non-compliance will be considered a serious breach of the work obligation in time of war. I think that's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The document date is 18th of -- 17th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That raises a point I wanted to raise, Your Honour, that the 17th July date doesn't appear to be on the English translation. I can see it there but I just would like to make sure the record reflects that. And also, the handwritten original, there's a word crossed out and I don't see that reflected in the translation as well. I don't know if Mr. Zecevic and the witness can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. Just allow me for a moment. First of all, at 58, 7, the date there is wrong, it says 1993, whereas in fact the date should be 17th of July, 1992. That is what we can see below the sentence strictly confidential, or rather, the abbreviation strictly confidential. Number 10-11/92. In the upper left corner of the document that is the date noted there, 17th of July 1992. As for the word that is crossed out, in the original text, Mr. Witness, could you please tell us, could you read this.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here, non-compliance with the issued order. The word "issued" is crossed out. Probably what was intended there was non-compliance with issued obligations or -- and then they probably put "orders" and then crossed out the "issued" so that that word was used to actually mean an order and that is reflected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, very well. If there is there are no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's time for the break so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, I wanted to tender the document if there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have an objection with those changes reflected on the record, but I don't know if you want to have it submitted to CLSS to have a revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we can have it MFI'd and then we'll -- pending translation from the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- I'm a little bit confused. You said the date of the document is 17 July. I read 18 on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, in the first -- if you look at the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- there is a 17 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Scrolled up, yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- and it says, By the 18th of July 1992 at 12 noon you have to submit the following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document marked at the end of the last session will become Exhibit 1D91, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Your Honours, we were instructed --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I do apologise, 1D91.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were instructed this morning to expedite our response in relation to the motion for amendment of subpoena by -- oh, but that has to be this closed session, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we go into private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, have you had time to look at the document that I've given to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call it up again. It's 65 ter 1483.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1483. 1483.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you if that was the meeting that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since we've already commented about it, I would just like to ask you something about what is on page 2 on the document that is seen on the e-court. The marking on the top of the page of that document is 012 [as interpreted] in the Serbian version. And we will look at item 2. So this is on the seconds page of the e-court document, both in the B/C/S and in the English.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the page which is marked 102?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 102, item 2 begins with Bosnia-Herzegovina will continue and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see there that Bosnia-Herzegovina shall continue to advocate the survival of a Yugoslav community on new foundations, which would be acceptable to all. In the meantime, it will also support the mutual co-operation between old institutions, thinking of the institutions of the federal state, but its representatives will not attend meetings of the Assembly in the Presidency of the SFRY unless they are attended by representatives of all the republics and the autonomous provinces. Decisions made in an incomplete session not attended by everyone will not be considered binding on Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is October 1991. At that time Slovenia and Croatia had already voted on and declared -- voted on their own declarations of independence; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if you permit me, this position clearly indicates that Bosnia and Herzegovina also will leave any kind of community in Yugoslavia even though it is presented in this form that we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have just anticipated my question so this, in fact, essentially means the obstruction of federal organs, although it is coached in this nice form, basically it signifies an obstruction of the federal organs in the sense that Bosnia-Herzegovina will leave the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is stated quite clearly. It says that, We support our common, joint organs but we will not participate in them unless Croatia and Slovenia participate in them too. But those two had already announced that they were going to not participate, so it means that they would not participate, and that also it says that decisions accepted without us will not be acceptable. And it is clearly stated in a way, it says, We are staying in Yugoslavia, but actually we have practically left it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you've looked at this document, does it accurately reflect the situation that prevailed during that period at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see the emotional charge that accompanies these key things that are being said. Much of that is important. The departure of the Serbian deputies, continuation of the work, adoption of decisions --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please -- I would like to have this document admitted into evidence. Just one moment, please. I was given the suggestion that on page 62 there is no division between my question and answer by Mr. Trbojevic. I think that my question ends on page 62, line 6, and that is where the answer by Mr. Trbojevic begins. So can we just please correct this now in the transcript. I apologise, it is -- on my LiveNote I have a different marking, so it is 62, 12. I'm being told that that is that -- page 62, line 12 is where my question ends and Mr. Trbojevic's answer begins. Thank you. Your Honours, if there is no objection, I would like to tender this document, the 65 ter 1483 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D92, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you joined the government in late May. I don't know if you are aware that the government, on the 24th of April, and it was signed by Mr. Djeric, issued some instruction on the conduct and the forming of Crisis Staffs. I don't know if you are aware of that. This is document P70.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were not in the government then, so the document is probably not familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the government but I had the opportunity to see this document later, and also to see the notification that it is being suspended very quickly after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is -- the document that suspended this bears the date the 27th of April, 1992, and it is marked in this case as P186. I'm not going to show you that document either because as you say, you were not a member of the government then, and this is already an exhibit in this case. What I wanted to show you is document P217. P217, and that is a record of a meeting from the government session of the 23rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can our -- our assistant can provide a hard copy of the document to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If it's an exhibit already in evidence, I don't need to see it. I trust, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a government meeting held on the 23rd of May. I assume that you also attended that session even though we don't have a record of those who were present at that time at government meetings. Can you please just glance over the document, maybe you remember that session? This could be the first or the second session that you would have attended perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I did attend, but to tell you the truth, I really couldn't tell you either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at item 4, the conclusion of the government. Item 4, it was concluded that measures should be taken to abolish the Crisis Staffs. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were probably familiar with the fact -- I mean, even those -- those Crisis Staffs didn't even function for a month and the government had already concluded that measures should be taken for their abolishment. You spoke a little bit about that, but the essence was that the government, or rather, the central authority practically could not, did not have control over the work of those Crisis Staffs and could not influence them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the gist of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that in the old Yugoslavia, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there was a Law on All People's Defence and Social Protection; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to show you in order not to burden the Trial Chamber with that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But for reference, that is the Law on All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection. This is 1D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D00-4042. But since all the legal documents will be stipulated between the parties, there's no need to tender these documents as separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that the Law on All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection provided for the creation of certain organ staffs, committees which took over the role of municipal organs in the event that due to different reasons, extraordinary circumstance, these organs are unable to convene. You are aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the basis of that law, these organs take upon themselves all the powers of the organs of powers for the period that the extraordinary circumstances are in effect and that also includes the sphere of defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the text of that regulation off by heart but I think that under the law, it was established who of the existing functionaries enters that organ and how that organ functions until the circumstances cease, due to which the organ was activated, and until the regular organs authorised for those particular duties again take these duties upon themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That organ, that law also laid down the powers of those organs and, what was a key point, it set a limited time-period for their work and their existence, i.e., until the extraordinary circumstances were valid or applied; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, are you aware that the Party of Democratic Action and it's leadership in the area, as well as the HDZ especially in Herceg-Bosnia and other places, had already formed their Crisis Staffs in their municipalities, these same types of organs, even before these organs started to be formed by the Serbian Democratic Party? Serbian Democratic Party, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that is more or less a matter of public knowledge. There was some testimony in these cases where it was noted that Crisis Staffs in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were formed on all three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From one of such cases, I got the information that at the time, in late 1991, in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were more than 950 different Crisis Staffs. This is in late 1991. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I know that they were in the hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina formed in September 1991 the Presidency Crisis Staff headed by Mr. Ejup Ganic, and whose members were the Defence minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Jerko Doko, the commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the minister of the interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Delimustafic, among others. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did see that. I saw the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to give a reference since you have confirmed that. This is 1D00-4585. This is a document, it's a Presidency record of a meeting where Mr. Alija Izetbegovic accepts to disband the Crisis Staff of the Presidency sometime in 1992, during negotiations with members of the Yugoslav People's Army. Mr. Trbojevic, you will agree with me, I hope, when I say that the need for such organs, such as the Crisis Staffs emerged because of the deep crisis that came about as far as the functioning of the central government and the regional or municipal authorities. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree that the crisis was deep, all encompassing and that you had to find a way to get out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A little bit earlier we looked at this document, these conclusions from the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina from October. It is evident that the obstruction by Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to the federal state, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was being reflected broadly within Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that the lower municipal organs were obstructing in the same way the central organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you agree with this assumption of mine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree that that is more or less what it was like, that the republics, one by one, were leaving the community, leaving the joint organs, the financing of the common budget. And in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were autonomous regions proclaimed, municipalities had suspended their payments of taxes, and participation in the budget contact, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that means that the total falling apart of the state system was considerably underway?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that that breaking apart and the destruction was proceeding from the top down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And these organs that were being formed in these extraordinary circumstances from that initial role of theirs to organise life in a territory during times of crisis and extraordinary circumstances with the deepening of the crisis and the escalation of the conflict suddenly became practically very powerful centres of power; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Local administration organs that were part of the system now became set apart from the system. They became independent and there was no other authority next to them, alongside them or above them so that they constituted the only power in a given area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Based on this process where they became a power in and of themselves, they began to issue orders to some organs which were absolutely incongruous [Realtime transcript read in error "in congress"] with the role of these bodies as originally envisaged?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These staffs took upon themselves the power to, for example, command a military unit that was like a local brigade or a local unit, the local police, which was not local by its structure and in it's main system because hierarchically it was connected to the state, but practically, there were people in the police station living in that particular area and they were subject to the authority of local power brokers. And this is now another question as to how this authority was imposed. Some places it functioned harmoniously, it varied from area to area. There were different circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In such circumstances and at times such as those, Republika Srpska in effect established its government of which you were the prime minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it is uncontested that the main stumbling block in the functioning of the government and the state was the fact that both the state and the government were being established under general wartime conditions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is obvious that the problem that we've just discussed, the problems relating to the Crisis Staff and the local centres of power, was something that was recognised early on by the central government, as early as May 1992, and then the Presidency, too, became aware of it because the Presidency made a decision to establish wartime presidencies in place of the Crisis Staffs. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is obvious that the government was trying to accomplish something. We can see that because there was -- that instruction from the month of April, but then it was withdrawn and the decision was made to establish wartime presidencies, which decision, in fact, exacerbated the situation, in my view, and I've said so on a number of occasions. I'd like to explain that. The Crisis Staff under the earlier provisions of the law on All People's Defence, they were established pursuant to that earlier law. The wartime presidencies, however, were established based on the realities on the ground for pragmatic reasons, and it became more obvious that people who had not been elected in the elections that had preceded were not becoming members of those bodies, but, rather, people who were members of the party saw that they were also now concentrating in their hands both the executive and the legislative powers they were taking upon themselves the powers that they were unable to actually sustain. And for pragmatic reasons, this was an attempt to actually hold under firm control by the party these powers, that's in my view at least as far as I could observe, and in fact that was a step back because it only led to further anarchy and lawlessness. Then there was the attempt to establish commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record and for the Trial Chamber, I would like to say that the decision on the establishment of wartime presidencies is document 65 ter 145. I don't know if it has already been exhibited in the meantime. That is 65 ter 145. If it hasn't already been admitted into evidence, perhaps we could show it to the witness. I don't have it in hard copy. Or rather, I'm sorry, this document is from the Official Gazette, so there is no reason to actually submit it now because it would be stipulated between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, one point, a correction for the transcript, I believe. On page 69, line 6, the transcript has the words "in congress" where I believe the -- it should be the single word "incongruous." Quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, sir, if I understand your evidence correctly, this decision on the establishment of wartime presidencies was actually an attempt at taking control over the Crisis Staffs and which, in your view, in fact only contributed to further chaos. So that it was followed by an amended decision and in place of the wartime presidencies, it was decided that wartime commissions should be established; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you are correct. Speaking about the ramifications and the consequences, I have to say that the decision on the establishment of these wartime presidencies also envisaged these commissioners to be their members and some sort of liaison between the central powers and the municipal authorities, the municipal bodies. But the commissioners who could not attend because they were at the other end of the world, as it were, and were unable to actually deal on a day-to-day basis with all these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there was -- there were situations where in some municipalities there were war commissions but the Crisis Staffs remained actually in operation. Do you know of any such cases?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were instances where there were all three types of bodies in operation at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said a moment ago a thing that I would like to examine now with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D60. And perhaps the usher can assist us, we have a hard copy of the document. 1D60. Six zero. Could the usher please assist me and provide the witness. I just need the last page. There is a comment that I would like to elicit or discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, before you see this document in a moment or so, let me just explain. This is a document, a report, from a collegium of the Ministry of the Interior, the date of the document is 16 November. It is dated the 16th of November, and this document was sent to everyone. This collegium of November 5, 1992, discussed topics relating to personnel issues within the Ministry of the Interior. I assume that you haven't seen this document before, but what I would like to ask you about is just a comment noted, a remark at the end of the document, the document which was signed by Mr. Stanisic, or rather, by someone on his behalf, and which remark reads as follows: "Due to the interference of the organs of the government and individuals within the Municipal Assemblies in the administrative policies of the SJB and CSB legal organs, Municipal Assemblies, will be informed thereof in a separate letter which is to follow." So even in mid-November, meaning immediately preceding the fall of the government, the Ministry of the Interior was dealing and had problems with the local organs, Crisis Staffs, commissioners, and similar, because they were interfering in personnel issues that were within the ambit of the Ministry of the Interior. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not really well acquainted with this, but I know there was situations where a number of these Crisis Staffs and municipal authorities, municipal administrations, sought to make sure that people who were, in their view, more malleable and more suitable enter these bodies, whether this was only because it was necessary to fill the positions that had been left vacant when the Muslims and Croats left, I don't know whether that was the reason, but there were various attempts within municipalities, but all of that was illegitimate, which we can actually read from this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, on a number of occasions today you mentioned this rift, the confrontation between Mr. Djeric, the president or the prime minister, and Mr. Stanisic. And you said, you described some clashes that you yourself witnessed, and so on and so forth. One of the things that I could infer from your testimony was that in effect neither you nor Mr. Stanisic at this point in time -- you yourself are unable to actually describe or explain what this conflict meant, how it had originated, and what it was about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that one of the rare ministries that really functioned or at least did their best to function optimally in this government, of which you were the deputy prime minister in this period between May and November 1992, was in fact the Ministry of the Interior, of course, compared to the work of the other ministries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the army actually, and that's a fact, managed to impose their own chain of command and structure, and it is also a fact that the Ministry of the Interior also implemented in the field their own structure and hierarchy. And in my view, this is a natural outcropping of their functions. All the other ministries were, in fact, administrative bodies. You had to find the person who would be the minister, and then you had to find their associates who would be willing to come up to Jahorina to begin with. And then there was the next step where you actually had to make them work. So both the military and the police had a very clear ambit of work and they had a clearly defined structure which naturally grew out of their -- of the nature of the service which -- because in each police station there was the structure and infrastructure as it normally existed, and your conclusion is quite correct that their structure was far more elaborate and far more complete than the structures of any of the other ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. One of the objections that Mr. Djeric put forth in these government sessions was the fact -- was to do with the fact that some of the ministers, including Mr. Stanisic, did not attend all government sessions. However, I would like to show you a document, that's 65 ter 1179 [as interpreted]. This is a government session of the 30th of May, 1992, at which time you were already a deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the last page of this document. Perhaps the usher could assist in providing a hard copy of this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think this is Exhibit P220 in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at this last page, that's page 5, the third paragraph from the bottom, where it says that the ministers are to appoint their deputies who will stand in for them in government sessions. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And for the most part, in most of these government sessions where Mr. Stanisic was absent, one of his deputies from the Ministry of the Interior always attended and there would be a remark stating that Mr. Stanisic was absent for official reasons; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could see that from these various minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we talked about the possible reasons for the clash between Mr. Djeric and Mr. Stanisic, I believe that my learned friend asked you something about a letter that Mr. Stanisic had sent to Mr. Djeric in the month of July 1992, and I believe that you said that you had never seen that letter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is document 65 ter 79, just for purposes of a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to show the document to you. Can we analyse now what you analysed with my learned friend in relation to the request or the conclusions of the government on the duties of the Ministry of the Interior, and to analyse a little bit what the ministry carried out of those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 1D496. I think the same document is the 65 ter document 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's an instruction by the prime minister, Branko Djeric, sent to the MUP, to the attention of the then undersecretary for public security matters, Mr. Cedomir Kljajic. This was on the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please just give Mr. Trbojevic the hard copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This refers to the government meeting of the 25th of May, 1992. Mr. Hannis also showed you this document a little bit earlier. This is a direct instruction issued from the prime minister, sent to the MUP, where it says that the government has concluded that it is necessary to submit information quickly about the security of people and property in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then, in parentheses, this refer especially to the facts relating to the vehicles from the TAS compound in Vogosca, the oil in Ilidza and the like. And then the prime minister continues that, after that, measures should be proposed. Did you see this document? Or do you remember seeing it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that it's my signature. I did sign it instead of the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it's your signature.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing new here in relation to what we talked about. There are numerous pieces of information about the attacks on the personal and property security, and then there was a special point about the Ilidza oil, the TAS Vogosca matter. These were two topics that were particularly current and immediate. They were evident and a lot of people were aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Because you signed this document, you evidently remember it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think this was initially when I came. You say that it was Cedo Kljajic. I have nothing to disagree with. I did hear about that -- the name. I probably could have had contacts with him, but I don't really recollect any contacts with him since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was going to say no objection, but I would indicate that I don't recall showing this document to the witness as Mr. Zecevic said in his testimony -- in his questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that I saw it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Probably it's a interpretation that is in question. I said that this relates to the conclusion of the government of the 25th of May, and that, if I recall, you showed him that record of the government meeting, the minutes meeting, where it was asked that information be provided regarding the TAS matter. This is only a written instruction to the MUP as a consequence of the decision by the government and I apologise for being imprecise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Registrar, please indicate the number of the -- 1D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at this document. This is document 1D62, and we have it here. We have a copy of it here for you. It's a document by the Ministry of the Interior of the 26th of May. The day after you sent that instruction out to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please just hand the document over to the witness so that you have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The document is dated the 26th of May. The previous instruction was of the 25th of May, this is the 26th of May, and it says in the first paragraph: "Since it is crucial that we urgently write a report for the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you are required to provide information about offences against people and property within the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then it lists what is expected to be contained in the report. On page 3 it says that the dead-line to submit the report is five days from then on, and that is the 31st of May, 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior acted pursuant to a conclusion by the government the following day after it received your dispatch; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now show the witness document which is an order, or rather, instruction of Mr. Goran Macar. This is 1D623 -- 1D00-0623.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That specifically relates to the issue of TAS and Vogosca --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's that document. Can we please give Mr. Trbojevic a copy of this document so he could look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska with the markings 02-16/92 of the 29th of July, 1992, although there is a mistake, doesn't matter, whatever the date is, the year is 1992. It's been delivered to the public security stations and to the minister of the MUP and information. It was signed by the administrator for the administration for crime prevention, Mr. Macar. This document is directly connected with that instruction and conclusion of the government regarding the TAS vehicles and parts that had disappeared. You can see in the first paragraph that: "In order to analyse the problems regarding theft of passenger vehicles from the TAS DP Vogosca and the theft of vehicles from the area of the SJBs, you are required to furnish the following information:" Then they request the list of -- stock list of the Vogosca company, information about the confiscated or stolen vehicles in other depots and warehouses, as well as the report from TAS on the number of vehicles the Crisis Staffs, companies, and other institutions which had taken vehicles. Then also the number of vehicles taken from other storage and warehouse facilities, the quantities still in stock, and so on and so forth. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the Ministry of the Interior in this case, too, is acting pursuant to conclusions and instructions of the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I've seen it before. It's not important if anyone has seen it or not, information is being requested here so what is necessary is to see the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Goran Macar as the head of the crime-fighting administration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of him. He is some sort of functionary. I don't know exactly what he was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections I would like to tender this document in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to request that this one be marked for identification at the moment. I think the author is scheduled as a witness later on in the case and there's nothing on the face of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's perfectly all right, Mr. Hannis. I accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D93, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please now show the witness document 65 ter 306.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch by Mr. Stanisic of the 23rd of August, 1992. Again it relates to TAS and it is a repeated instruction by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please ask the usher to hand the document over to the witness. [In English] Yes, I know it's in e-court, but I believe Mr. Trbojevic said that he is experiencing some problems in following the documents with the monitor. He said something with the glasses, but that's why I provided the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I'm creating any problem. I believe Mr. Hannis was assisting the witness in the same manner. That is why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- I tried to accommodate the witness. That is the only reason I'm providing him with hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand that we have a cable problem that the process that both of you followed is accommodating, so we have no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Trbojevic, this is a document by the MUP in Sarajevo, number 10-259/92, and it is dated the 23rd of August, 1992. It was dispatched to the CSB in Sarajevo, the department for crime prevention and detection. It's signed, you will see, by -- or for Mr. Stanisic. I'm not sure if it is his signature, but in any case, it is signed and stamped by the Ministry of Interior. The document states that the prevention of criminal offences was discussed again at the 47th Session of the government of the Serb republics held on the 20th of August, 1992, and it was concluded that: "It was high time that the MUP compiles a report on the theft of Golf-made cars from TAS and on the necessity to start confiscating booty. There was also talk of there being another 300 of these Golf vehicles and that a new 'channel' was opened in the direction of Kiseljak." Then the MUP asked the CSB on whose territory the TAS factory in Vogosca is located to compile a report about the to date work. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, the Ministry of the Interior constitutes that there is insufficient activity of the Sarajevo CSB and that has brought into question the legal safety of citizens and the confidence into the rule of law, and that is why it is necessary that the Sarajevo CSB compiles a detailed report on the measures to prevent crime with statistic indicators and so on and so forth. And in the last paragraph it says the dead-line to submit information about the theft of Golfs from the TAS and other information is the 28th of August, 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of that is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that after the criticism by the government on the 47th -- at the 47th Session, there was a reaction by the Ministry of the Interior, and again a request seeking information from the Sarajevo CSB which evidently did not act pursuant to the previous request?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no objection, I would like to tender this document. Mr. Hannis, perhaps we can also MFI the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I know you said you didn't know whether it was your client's signature or signed by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree. I suggest the document be marked for identification, and then when Mr. Macar comes, we are going to see about the document with him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D94, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you another document now that deals with TAS and these Golfs and I think that it's an important document in order to potentially indicate where the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is document 65 ter 1350. And I would like to ask the usher to give the witness a hard copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, while we wait for the document to come up, please tell us, do you know Mr. Nikola Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 1350.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that Mr. Poplasen was the republic commissioner for Vogosca municipality, are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, here we have before us a document produced by Mr. Poplasen, and signed by him, of June 24th, I believe, 1992. The heading is "Wartime Presidency," and I assume this relates to Vogosca municipality, and it reads as follows: "After the evaluation of the current situation on the territory of Serbian municipality Vogosca, at this point in time, I suggest that the following initiatives be implemented." Under 1, ensure the sale of TAS products, in parentheses Golf and Caddy, these are types of vehicles; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The sale of these products on Serbian and Montenegrin markets for stable currency or goods that we are interested in, this task should be given, we can't read clearly here, and an expert group from TAS and Vogosca, and so and on and so forth. Now, you can see here that in June 1992, the Wartime Presidency, it would appear, is taking initiative and seeking to sell these vehicles. Was the government aware of such an initiative?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And did you know that the Wartime Presidency was implementing this initiative, selling these vehicles in Serbia and Montenegro for hard currency or for some barter agreements? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know -- can you recognise Mr. Poplasen's signature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really say that. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, this being the Prosecutor's document, I don't know if we should MFI it and wait for a witness who can actually authenticate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the moment I would request it be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D95, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you said earlier today, during examination-in-chief, that you are aware that at a later point in time this complete report was actually submitted to a later government and Presidency, but that it was not complete, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said something to that effect. There was a report submitted but I don't know how it was actually implemented in the final stages. I don't know if anyone was found guilty of this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in any case, in the government -- in your government, the government of Mr. Djeric, which went on until November 1992, and in the course of 1992 in any case, that such a report was not submitted either to the government or to the Assembly, correct, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you be very brief in your answers, we just have five or six more minutes. But you being an expert on these matters, tell us, please, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, in our system, it is part of the state administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Our system also classifies -- there's a certain classification within our system of administration, communications, and documents that they produce?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there are regulations as it to the type of document that a certain administration or body can produce and what their meaning is, and I think that this was stipulated in the Law on Government Administration. I think the names of such documents and their ranking was provided for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As the Ministry of the Interior was part of the government or state administration, it was also subject to the Law on State Administration and also subject to the Law on the General Administrative Procedure in executing its powers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When speaking about these documents and enactments, I will name a few and I would like you to confirm for us whether these are administrative enactments. So rules of procedure; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, rules of procedure are an administrative enactment of the highest order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, instructions are -- I'm not certain right now whether the law defines it as an act of the -- of an administrative body, but in practice it was very common and it would provide practical instructions as to how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about written decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Written decisions are enactments that define a certain right, so they are decisions basically, which implies that there was a procedure in place, that there is also the right to appeal that written decision and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you can agree with me that an order is, in fact, the lowest ranking. In this nomenclature, this is an enactment of the lowest rank or lowest order and its effect is the weakest?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that sense, it is an enactment of the lowest order, and it in fact defines, for instance, the scheduling or timing of a certain procedure and so on. So it does not really decide on anything. It's not a decision-making enactment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, your last sentence was not actually recorded in the transcript, and it in fact answered my question. So what is the difference between this order and a military order, because in the Serbian language we use the same word, the identical word, but if I understood you correctly, there was a very important difference between an order of an administrative body and a military order.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly -- that's what I just said. I wasn't really looking at the text. But a decision issued by a superior to a subordinate in the army is an enactment that implies subordination and is obligatory. It has to be executed. Whereas an order of the administrative body is a process or procedural enactment that does not decide anything. It is just something that, for instance, calls for a scheduling or calls for a meeting to be held on so and so day, and so on. So there is no implied obligation to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honours, I believe that this would be a good moment to break up for the day because we are moving on to another topic, and I'm pretty certain that we will finish our cross-examination in the course of the first session tomorrow. This is for my learned friend's information and for the Trial Chamber's. Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic, we will resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Trbojevic, I would again, as I would have done yesterday, remind you of the fact that having been sworn, you -- your communications are limited. Thank you. So we resume in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
